newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Cenbank says forex system won't change.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Cenbank says forex system won't change.

text.p: Central Bank director Gustavo Franco said Brazil was not considering any change in its foreign exchange policy amid growing speculation of an alteration in the current band system.
"There is no change in the foreign exchange policy... It's all speculation," Franco told reporters at a conference of Latin American utilities.
Although Franco said no change was under way, he noted, "It's better to work with a large band." He did not elaborate.

Franco's comments follow several days of speculation in the Brazilian press that the bank was preparing to eliminate the use of the so-called "large band," within which the reais currency trades against the dollar over a period of 12 months or more.

The reais trades daily against the dollar within the "mini-band," which the Central Bank depreciates about six times a month. The real has depreciated against the dollar by between 0.50 percent and 0.65 percent each month over the past several months.
News reports said the bank was considering eliminating the large band and widening the mini-band to free up trading in the spot dollar market and reduce speculation in the futures market.
Brazil's reais currency is now trading at between 1.0485 reais and 1.0535 reais per dollar, approaching the ceiling of the existing 0.97-1.06 large band, which was set on January 30, 1996.

This has led to expectations of an imminent widening of the large band to between 1.05 reais and 1.12 reais, for example. Such a move would be consistent with Brazil's current forex policy and would not signal a change of plan by the Central Bank, economists said.

But some in the market have speculated that this time around, the Central Bank may simply eliminate the large band and rely exclusively on one band whose spread would be somewhere between those of the existing mini and large bands.
"The large band doesn't mean anything. The forex rate follows the mini-band," one trader said.
Still, most market players say that the Central Bank normally acts cautiously and that whatever it decided to do it would probably not have a strong impact on current exchange rate depreciation.
The Central Bank depreciated the real by 6.9 percent against the dollar in 1996 and the market expects a similar rate of devaluation this year.
